title: Adding Inputs in Time and Space

scenes.tts: Two inputs arrive ten milliseconds apart. Does the second start from rest, or from what the first left behind?
scenes.caption: Two inputs arrive 10 ms apart. Does the second start from rest, or from what the first left behind?
scenes.visual: Two small arrows on a time axis, 10 ms apart, above a flat Vm trace at −65 mV. A question mark between them.
scenes.narration: Two inputs arrive 10 ms apart. Does the second start from rest, or from what the first left behind?

scenes.tts: When conductances change, the marker does not jump to the new balance point. It moves there gradually.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale from chapter 1. A ghost marker labelled balance point jumps right; the real marker follows smoothly behind it.
scenes.narration: When conductances change, the marker does not jump to the new balance point. It moves there gradually.

scenes.tts: Changing the voltage means moving charge onto or off the membrane's capacitance. That takes time.
scenes.visual: The membrane drawn as two plates (a capacitor), C, with charges flowing onto it while the marker moves.
scenes.narration: Changing the voltage means moving charge onto or off the membrane's capacitance. That takes time.

scenes.tts: The membrane time constant, tau, says how long. It is the time to get 63 percent of the way to a new voltage.
scenes.caption: The membrane time constant, τ, says how long. It is the time to get 63% of the way to a new voltage.
scenes.visual: A rising exponential trace with a dashed line at 63% of the way to the new level, and the time to reach it marked τ.
scenes.narration: The membrane time constant, τ, says how long. It is the time to get 63% of the way to a new voltage.

scenes.tts: Tau equals the capacitance divided by the total open conductance. In our cell, that is 20 milliseconds.
scenes.caption: τ equals the capacitance divided by the total open conductance. In our cell, that is 20 ms.
scenes.visual: On screen only: τ = C / total g = 200 pF / 10 nS = 20 ms. Also: R = 1/gL = 100 MΩ.
scenes.narration: τ equals the capacitance divided by the total open conductance. In our cell, that is 20 ms.

scenes.tts: Because tau uses the total conductance, in this passive model every synapse that opens shortens it.
scenes.caption: Because τ uses the total conductance, in this passive model every synapse that opens shortens it.
scenes.visual: On screen: τ_eff = C / (gL + gE + gI). The bottom line grows as a new rope appears; τ shrinks.
scenes.narration: Because τ uses the total conductance, in this passive model every synapse that opens shortens it.

scenes.tts: So an EPSP has a shape. For a brief, fast input in our cell, it rises while synaptic current flows, over a few milliseconds.
scenes.visual: Above, a synaptic current pulse lasting a few ms, labelled 'synaptic current flows'. Below, a single EPSP trace rising during the pulse. Label: brief fast input, compact passive cell.
scenes.narration: So an EPSP has a shape. For a brief, fast input in our cell, it rises while synaptic current flows, over a few milliseconds.

scenes.tts: Once that current fades, the voltage decays back toward rest, with the resting time constant.
scenes.visual: The current pulse has ended; the same EPSP's slow exponential decay is highlighted and labelled τ. Small print: other receptors, dendrites and active channels give other shapes.
scenes.narration: Once that current fades, the voltage decays back toward rest, with the resting time constant.

scenes.tts: If a second EPSP arrives before the first has gone, it starts from the first one's tail. That is temporal summation.
scenes.visual: A second EPSP starts on the tail of the first; its peak sits higher. Label: temporal summation.
scenes.narration: If a second EPSP arrives before the first has gone, it starts from the first one's tail. That is temporal summation.

scenes.tts: Two brief, idealized pulses arrive ten milliseconds apart. Each jumps the voltage by two millivolts. Cell A has a tau of 20 milliseconds. Cell B's is 10. Which ends higher?
scenes.caption: Two brief, idealized pulses arrive 10 ms apart. Each jumps the voltage by 2 mV. Cell A has a τ of 20 ms. Cell B's is 10 ms. Which ends higher?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. Two 0.4 pC pulses, 10 ms apart, each a 2 mV jump. Cell A: τ = 20 ms. Cell B: τ = 10 ms. Which is higher just after pulse 2? Two empty trace panels side by side.
scenes.narration: Two brief, idealized pulses arrive 10 ms apart. Each jumps the voltage by 2 mV. Cell A has a τ of 20 ms. Cell B's is 10 ms. Which ends higher?

scenes.tts: Cell A. After ten milliseconds, its first EPSP has decayed only to about 61 percent. The second lands on top of that.
scenes.caption: Cell A. After 10 ms, its first EPSP has decayed only to about 61%. The second lands on top of that.
scenes.visual: Cell A's panel draws two EPSPs; the tail at the second pulse is highlighted. On screen only: 2 + 2 × e^(−10/20) = 3.21 mV.
scenes.narration: Cell A. After 10 ms, its first EPSP has decayed only to about 61%. The second lands on top of that.

scenes.tts: Cell B's first EPSP has fallen to about 37 percent. So cell A ends a little over three millivolts, and cell B under three.
scenes.caption: Cell B's first EPSP has fallen to about 37%. So cell A ends a little over 3 mV, and cell B under 3 mV.
scenes.visual: Cell B's panel draws two EPSPs with a shorter tail. On screen only: 2 + 2 × e^(−10/10) = 2.74 mV. The two peaks are compared with a bracket.
scenes.narration: Cell B's first EPSP has fallen to about 37%. So cell A ends a little over 3 mV, and cell B under 3 mV.

scenes.tts: A longer tau leaves a longer tail, and that means more summation. Remember cell B. It returns later in this lesson.
scenes.caption: A longer τ leaves a longer tail, and that means more summation. Remember cell B. It returns later in this lesson.
scenes.visual: Card: longer τ → longer tail → more summation. Cell B's panel gets a small bookmark tag.
scenes.narration: A longer τ leaves a longer tail, and that means more summation. Remember cell B. It returns later in this lesson.

scenes.tts: Now distance. Most synapses sit on dendrites, not on the cell body.
scenes.visual: A neuron drawing: a soma with a long dendrite. A synapse icon sits partway along the dendrite.
scenes.narration: Now distance. Most synapses sit on dendrites, not on the cell body.

scenes.tts: Current entering a dendrite flows toward the soma. But some leaks out across the membrane along the way.
scenes.visual: Current arrows flow along the dendrite toward the soma, with small arrows leaking out through the dendrite's wall.
scenes.narration: Current entering a dendrite flows toward the soma. But some leaks out across the membrane along the way.

scenes.tts: In a long, uniform passive dendrite, a steady voltage change shrinks by the same fraction over each equal stretch.
scenes.visual: A long uniform dendrite, labelled 'long, uniform, passive'. A bump drawn above it shrinks step by step at equal intervals toward the soma.
scenes.narration: In a long, uniform passive dendrite, a steady voltage change shrinks by the same fraction over each equal stretch.

scenes.tts: The length constant, lambda, is the distance over which it falls to 37 percent.
scenes.caption: The length constant, λ, is the distance over which it falls to 37%.
scenes.visual: An exponential decay curve above the dendrite, with the 37% point marked at one λ. On screen: V(x) = V0 × e^(−x/λ).
scenes.narration: The length constant, λ, is the distance over which it falls to 37%.

scenes.tts: Put a synapse half a length constant from the soma. About 61 percent of its steady depolarization arrives.
scenes.caption: Put a synapse half a length constant from the soma. About 61% of its steady depolarization arrives.
scenes.visual: On screen only: λ = 500 µm, synapse at 250 µm, e^(−0.5) = 0.61. The bump at the soma is 61% of the bump at the synapse.
scenes.narration: Put a synapse half a length constant from the soma. About 61% of its steady depolarization arrives.

scenes.tts: A brief EPSP loses more, because capacitance along the way also filters it.
scenes.visual: A brief EPSP travels the same path and arrives smaller and broader.
scenes.narration: A brief EPSP loses more, because capacitance along the way also filters it.

scenes.tts: Adding inputs at different places is spatial summation. For the same local change, inputs near the soma, or on dendrites with a long lambda, lose less.
scenes.caption: Adding inputs at different places is spatial summation. For the same local change, inputs near the soma, or on dendrites with a long λ, lose less.
scenes.visual: Two synapses on different dendrites send bumps to the soma, where they add. Label: spatial summation. Small print: same local change, other things equal.
scenes.narration: Adding inputs at different places is spatial summation. For the same local change, inputs near the soma, or on dendrites with a long λ, lose less.

scenes.tts: Time and distance decide how much of each input is still there when the cell decides. The balance point decides what they add up to.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: τ and λ decide how much of each input is left. The balance point decides what the inputs add up to.
scenes.narration: Time and distance decide how much of each input is still there when the cell decides. The balance point decides what they add up to.
